Accuracy is normally stated as a percentage of reading, so a tight figure only helps if low-flow behaviour is also good. Nominal pipe size sets the ceiling of the usable range, not the floor. A suite branch illustrates why the lower end of the range deserves attention.

A Four-Step Sizing Method

  1. List fixture demand: Estimate the combined flow from toilet fills, showers, faucets, and appliances on the branch. Use realistic simultaneous demand, not the pipe's theoretical capacity.
  2. Find the night baseline: Measure or estimate the smallest overnight flow that needs to register. Set any leak alert threshold above normal background use.
  3. Check the meter's range: Compare the candidate's minimum and maximum flow limits with both the night baseline and expected peak. This overview of copper pipe diameters can help distinguish nominal pipe size from the meter's usable range.
  4. Keep normal demand in range: Select a meter that measures routine use within its effective range and can still register the flow relevant to leak detection.

Size hot and cold services separately. Their demand patterns can differ, and a meter that suits a cold-water branch may operate too high or too low in the range on a hot-water branch. Pressure conditions also affect the flow delivered by fixtures, so account for the actual installation.

OIML R 49 distinguishes between lower- and higher-flow zones. Its lower-flow zone permits up to ±5% maximum permissible error, with tighter limits at higher flows, as summarized in the OIML R 49 metering requirements summary. That figure is a maximum permissible error, or MPE, under the standard. Municipal test or acceptance windows use a different convention: they state the range of measured results that qualify for acceptance. Those windows are not directly comparable to an MPE limit.

Suite-level submetering fails when the ultrasonic meter's minimum flow sits above a toilet leak. You've paid for resolution you didn't get. Confirm the threshold against the leak you care about, not against a catalogue turndown ratio.

Irrigation branches suit electromagnetic meters because there's no rotor for debris to jam. The failure mode is different. If the water isn't sufficiently conductive, or grounding is poor, readings drift or drop out entirely.

Large commercial makeup lines also favour electromagnetic designs, since accuracy holds as size grows. Budget for power, grounding rings, and liner selection. Those costs surprise owners who priced only the flow tube.

Hot-water recirculation loops need ultrasonic sensors rated for sustained hot service. A meter specified for cold water and installed on a recirculation loop can fail early, even if its flow range looks right.

Steady building supplies can suit vortex meters, provided flow stays above minimum velocity and you have the straight run. Put a vortex meter on a low-demand branch and it reads nothing below that velocity. It isn't broken. It's out of range.

Low-cost branches are the honest home for turbine or paddlewheel meters. Use them where error tolerance is wide and nobody expects leak detection. A paddlewheel on a suite branch will miss toilet leaks by design, so don't assign it that job.

How Installation Changes Meter Performance

Straight-run requirements exist because meters infer flow from a velocity profile, and that profile needs distance to settle after a disturbance.

Disturbances, Air, and Hydraulics

Upstream elbows, pumps, and partly open valves create swirl and uneven velocity profiles that bias ultrasonic and vortex readings. The meter reports a number confidently. Practical rule: If you can't isolate and remove a meter without shutting down the building, you don't have a maintenance plan. You have a future outage.

Install isolation valves and bypass provisions where permitted, and plan power and grounding for electromagnetic meters before the ceiling closes. Retrofitting those details costs far more than drawing them.
